notes: All regional forms are draft proposals awaiting content review.
The fixed synthetic benchmark scale is one EUR per source monetary unit; it is not a live exchange rate.
Spanish uses Latin script: native and romanized display forms retain the same diacritics. Machine email local parts may be ASCII.
Internal identifiers, task membership, scenario clock ordering, numerical predicates and reward intent remain unchanged.
Existing locale corpus and identity maps are reference material; their prior annotations do not validate new regional forms.

decisions.source_assessment: The English source "Junius Buckminster-Chavel" is harder than the same-family Easy sources such as intake_person_names_easy_01 "Lisa Sandoval", intake_person_names_easy_02 "Michael Santiago", and intake_person_names_easy_07 "Sandra Carter": it combines an uncommon given name, a long uncommon surname component, a hyphenated final component, close written decoys "Chaver"/"Justus", and explicit nontrivial pronunciation distortions for three tokens. The source semantics can support a hard localized person-name capture task.

hazards.evidence: The caller first says only "Julián" under the omission instruction, while the true value is the three-part hyphenated name "Julián Bescós-Chacel".
hazards.resolving_clarification: «El nombre completo es Julián Bescós-Chacel: Julián, apellido Bescós guion Chacel.»

hazards.evidence: "Bescós-Chacel" contains an accented surname component and an uncommon second component; it can be confused with the decoy "Bescós-Chacón" or lose the accent in "Bescós".
hazards.resolving_clarification: «Bescós lleva tilde en la o: B-e-s-c-ó-s; después guion y Chacel, C-h-a-c-e-l.»

hazards.evidence: The supplied native pronunciation contrasts "Chacel" with distorted "Chocel" and the decoy "Chacón"; a vowel or final syllable mishearing changes the written surname.
hazards.resolving_clarification: «Es Chacel, con a en la primera sílaba y terminado en -cel, no Chacón ni Chocel.»

decisions.comparison_to_easy: Compared with the Easy controls, this localized case adds a recoverable hyphenated surname and uncommon components. intake_person_names_easy_01 "Laura Sandoval", easy_02 "Miguel Santiago", easy_07 "Sandra Cortés", and easy_10 "Susana Jiménez" are ordinary two-token names with no pronunciation dependency and no hyphenated surname; even easy_04 "Javier Herrera" only adds a simple double-rr spelling style. "Julián Bescós-Chacel" requires capturing the omitted surname, the hyphen boundary, the accent in Bescós, and the uncommon Chacel/Chacón distinction.

decisions.source_assessment: The English source "Heyward Golle-Medora" is hard relative to Easy sources like intake_person_names_easy_03 "Michelle Meyer", intake_person_names_easy_06 "Steven Singh", and intake_person_names_easy_09 "Linda Dunn": it has uncommon name forms, a hyphenated surname, a double-letter spelling style for "Golle", close written decoys "Medart"/"Reynard", and explicit pronunciation traps. The source is not merely long; it creates real spelling and component-boundary capture risk.

hazards.evidence: The localized answer "Heriberto Gálvez-Medrano" is a full name with a hyphenated double surname, but the caller initially gives only "Heriberto".
hazards.resolving_clarification: «El nombre completo es Heriberto Gálvez-Medrano: Heriberto, apellido Gálvez guion Medrano.»

hazards.evidence: "Gálvez-Medrano" requires the accent in "Gálvez" and the exact second surname "Medrano", which is close to the written decoy "Gálvez-Mediano".
hazards.resolving_clarification: «Gálvez lleva tilde en la a: G-á-l-v-e-z; después guion Medrano, M-e-d-r-a-n-o.»

hazards.evidence: The native pronunciation dependency contrasts "Gálvez" with "Gólvez" and "Medrano" with "Mendrano"; these are audible vowel/consonant changes that could produce a wrong surname.
hazards.resolving_clarification: «Es Gálvez con a, y Medrano sin n después de la e: Me-dra-no.»

decisions.comparison_to_easy: This is harder than the Easy controls because it combines a less common given name and a hyphenated two-part surname with accent and internal consonant risks. intake_person_names_easy_02 "Miguel Santiago", easy_06 "Esteban Sanz", and easy_09 "Lidia Durán" are two-token names; easy_04 "Javier Herrera" has a double-rr spelling style but no hyphenated surname. "Heriberto Gálvez-Medrano" adds the Gálvez accent, the Gálvez/Medrano boundary, and Medrano versus Mediano/Mendrano capture hazards.

decisions.source_assessment: The English source "Giuseppe Lansbury-Cutugno" is hard independently of its label: "Giuseppe" and "Cutugno" have non-obvious English pronunciations, "Lansbury-Cutugno" is hyphenated, the task includes a double-letter spelling style for "Giuseppe", and the decoys target both the given name and the final surname. This is materially harder than Easy sources such as intake_person_names_easy_01 "Lisa Sandoval", easy_05 "Jennifer McDonald", and easy_08 "Thomas Henry", which are simpler two-component names.

hazards.evidence: The true localized value is "Gustavo Lanuza-Cutiño", but the scripted first response supplies only "Gustavo"; the surname must later be recovered as the hyphenated "Lanuza-Cutiño".
hazards.resolving_clarification: «El nombre completo es Gustavo Lanuza-Cutiño, con el apellido Lanuza guion Cutiño.»

hazards.evidence: "Cutiño" contains the Spanish ñ, and the written decoy "Gustavo Lanuza-Cuetiño" inserts an extra e after Cu-; both affect the normalized written answer.
hazards.resolving_clarification: «Cutiño se escribe C-u-t-i-ñ-o, con eñe y sin e después de la u.»

hazards.evidence: "Lanuza" versus distorted "Lanusa" relies on the z/s distinction in Spain, and "Cutiño" versus "Cutino" relies on ñ versus n; both are audible but easy to lose in capture.
hazards.resolving_clarification: «Es Lanuza con zeta, no con ese; y Cutiño con eñe.»

decisions.comparison_to_easy: Relative to the Easy controls, "Gustavo Lanuza-Cutiño" adds a hyphenated surname, a z/s spelling distinction, and ñ capture. intake_person_names_easy_03 "Marta Moreno", easy_05 "Jimena Macías", and easy_08 "Tomás Herrera" are standard two-token names; although some Easy items contain accents, they do not require resolving a hyphen boundary plus ñ and zeta/ese distinctions. The caller can recover the exact value by spelling the surname components.

decisions.source_assessment: The English source "Barclay Marilla-Freston" is a real hard source relative to Easy controls such as intake_person_names_easy_04 "Jeffrey Harper", easy_07 "Sandra Carter", and easy_10 "Susan Jenkins": it uses uncommon components, a hyphenated surname, a double-letter spelling style for "Marilla", close decoys "Fredson"/"Bartley", and pronunciation distortions based on metathesis and vowel changes. The hard effect is not just length; it requires distinguishing component boundaries and exact spellings.

hazards.evidence: The localized full answer "Beltrán Marín-Fresneda" has a hyphenated surname, while the caller initially says only "Beltrán".
hazards.resolving_clarification: «El nombre completo es Beltrán Marín-Fresneda: Beltrán, apellido Marín guion Fresneda.»

hazards.evidence: "Beltrán" and "Marín" both contain accents, and the surname "Marín-Fresneda" can be confused with the decoy "Merino-Fresneda" if the first surname is not spelled.
hazards.resolving_clarification: «Beltrán lleva tilde en la a; Marín lleva tilde en la i: M-a-r-í-n; después guion Fresneda.»

hazards.evidence: The pronunciation examples contrast "Beltrán" with "Bertlán", "Marín" with "Morín", and "Fresneda" with "Fersneda"; these are audible reorderings or vowel changes that can lead to a wrong written capture.
hazards.resolving_clarification: «Es Beltrán, no Bertlán; Marín con a; y Fresneda, F-r-e-s-n-e-d-a.»

decisions.comparison_to_easy: The Easy controls, for example intake_person_names_easy_01 "Laura Sandoval", easy_04 "Javier Herrera", easy_07 "Sandra Cortés", and easy_10 "Susana Jiménez", are simple given-name-plus-surname captures; easy_04 has a double-rr spelling style but no hyphenated surname or multiple accents. decisions.source_assessment: The English source "Valentino Barloon-Olayan" is hard relative to Easy sources such as intake_person_names_easy_02 "Michael Santiago", easy_05 "Jennifer McDonald", and easy_09 "Linda Dunn": it has a long uncommon hyphenated surname, the double-vowel component "Barloon", close decoys "Olason"/"Valentin", a double-letter spelling style, and pronunciation distortions for every token. These create genuine spelling and boundary hazards.

hazards.evidence: The true localized value is "Valentín Barriopedro-Olalla", but the caller initially gives only "Valentín"; the missing surname is long and hyphenated.
hazards.resolving_clarification: «El nombre completo es Valentín Barriopedro-Olalla: Valentín, apellido Barriopedro guion Olalla.»

hazards.evidence: "Valentín" requires an accent, "Barriopedro" contains rr, and "Olalla" contains ll; the decoy "Valentín Barriopedro-Olaya" differs in the ll/y spelling even if it may sound the same under yeísmo.

hazards.evidence: The native dependencies include vowel contrasts "Valentín"/"Valentón", "Barriopedro"/"Borriopedro", and "Olalla"/"Ololla"; these audible vowel changes can mislead capture before spelling is requested.
hazards.resolving_clarification: «Es Valentín con i, Barriopedro con a al principio, y Olalla con a: O-la-lla.»

decisions.comparison_to_easy: This localized case is harder than the Easy set because it adds a long hyphenated surname with rr and ll spelling clarification. intake_person_names_easy_02 "Miguel Santiago", easy_05 "Jimena Macías", and easy_09 "Lidia Durán" are two-token names; easy_04 "Javier Herrera" has only the simpler double-rr issue in one surname. "Valentín Barriopedro-Olalla" requires recovering the omitted surname, preserving the hyphen boundary, and clarifying rr/ll plus the accent in Valentín.

decisions.source_assessment: The English source is harder than the same-family Easy controls because “Eldora Colier” uses an uncommon given name and a non-obvious surname spelling/pronunciation, with close decoys “Eldora Collea” and “Elnora Colier” plus pronunciation traps for both tokens. This is materially harder than Easy sources such as “Lisa Sandoval” in intake_person_names_easy_01 or “Michael Santiago” in intake_person_names_easy_02, which are common two-token names without pronunciation examples.

hazards.evidence: The initial caller gives only “Elvira”; the recoverable full answer is “Elvira Cañizares-Montesinos”, so the agent must elicit and capture a compound hyphenated family name rather than a single surname.
hazards.resolving_clarification: “El nombre completo es Elvira Cañizares-Montesinos; el apellido es Cañizares guion Montesinos.”

hazards.evidence: “Cañizares” contains “ñ”, which can be missed or normalized to “Canizares”; the supplied pronunciation contrast explicitly lists distorted “Canizares”.
hazards.resolving_clarification: “Cañizares se escribe C-A-Ñ-I-Z-A-R-E-S, con eñe.”

hazards.evidence: “Cañizares-Montesinos” requires preserving the hyphen and boundary between the two surname components; otherwise it may be captured as one run-on surname or as two unhyphenated surnames.
hazards.resolving_clarification: “Después de Cañizares va un guion y luego Montesinos.”

decisions.comparison_to_easy: Compared with intake_person_names_easy_01 “Laura Sandoval”, intake_person_names_easy_02 “Miguel Santiago”, and intake_person_names_easy_07 “Sandra Cortés”, the localized hard case keeps the same lazy-omission pattern but adds a naturally plausible compound surname “Cañizares-Montesinos”, an “ñ” spelling hazard, and a hyphen boundary that the Easy controls do not require. It is also harder than intake_person_names_easy_04 “Javier Herrera”, where the only extra spelling style is a simple double-r/“doble erre” convention.

decisions.source_assessment: The English source “Archibald Hellerman-Ratican” is independently hard: it is a long, uncommon multi-component name with a hyphenated surname, close decoys affecting both the given name and the final component, and pronunciation traps for “Archibald”, “Hellerman”, and “Ratican”. This is harder than Easy sources such as “Thomas Henry” in intake_person_names_easy_08 or “Sandra Carter” in intake_person_names_easy_07, which are short two-token names without pronunciation dependencies.

hazards.evidence: “Arquímedes Valderrama-Riaza” has a rare given name plus a hyphenated family name; after the scripted omission the caller initially says only “Arquímedes”, so the full answer requires eliciting “Valderrama-Riaza”.
hazards.resolving_clarification: “El nombre completo es Arquímedes Valderrama-Riaza; el apellido es Valderrama guion Riaza.”

hazards.evidence: “Arquímedes” contains an accented í, and “Valderrama” contains double rr; the spelling style instructs “doble erre”, so the agent must capture the written form rather than a simplified version.
hazards.resolving_clarification: “Arquímedes lleva tilde en la i; Valderrama se escribe V-A-L-D-E doble erre A-M-A.”

hazards.evidence: The boundary in “Valderrama-Riaza” matters: the decoy “Arquímedes Valderrama-Riazo” differs only in the final vowel of the second component, and the hyphen must be preserved.
hazards.resolving_clarification: “Es Riaza, con a final: Valderrama guion Riaza.”

decisions.comparison_to_easy: The Easy controls such as intake_person_names_easy_01 “Laura Sandoval”, intake_person_names_easy_06 “Esteban Sanz”, and intake_person_names_easy_08 “Tomás Herrera” require at most a single family name after omission. Even intake_person_names_easy_04 “Javier Herrera” only adds a double-r spelling convention. This case adds a rare accented given name, a double-r surname, and a second hyphenated surname component “Riaza”, making native-script capture substantially harder.

decisions.source_assessment: The English source “Manley Luvian-Berlet” is hard because it contains uncommon or coined-looking tokens, a hyphenated surname, close decoys “Manley Luvian-Berlew” and “Mandel Luvian-Berlet”, and pronunciation traps for all three source tokens. This is harder than the Easy English names like “Linda Dunn” in intake_person_names_easy_09 or “Susan Jenkins” in intake_person_names_easy_10, which are familiar two-token names with no comparable multi-token pronunciation burden.

hazards.evidence: “Melanio Luján-Bermejo” contains a less common given name and a hyphenated surname; the first utterance gives only “Melanio”, so the agent must recover “Luján-Bermejo” through follow-up.
hazards.resolving_clarification: “El nombre completo es Melanio Luján-Bermejo; el apellido es Luján guion Bermejo.”

hazards.evidence: “Luján” contains an accented á, and the decoy “Luján-Bercejo” shows that the second component “Bermejo” must be captured exactly, not just approximately.
hazards.resolving_clarification: “Luján lleva tilde en la a; Bermejo se escribe B-E-R-M-E-J-O.”

hazards.evidence: The hyphen in “Luján-Bermejo” is a required boundary between two surname components; without clarification it could be entered as two unhyphenated surnames or as a single combined string.
hazards.resolving_clarification: “Entre Luján y Bermejo va un guion.”

decisions.comparison_to_easy: Compared with intake_person_names_easy_05 “Jimena Macías” and intake_person_names_easy_09 “Lidia Durán”, which include an accent but only one family-name token, this localized case adds a compound hyphenated surname “Luján-Bermejo” and a second surname component whose spelling is tested by the decoy “Bercejo”. It is also more demanding than intake_person_names_easy_01 “Laura Sandoval” and intake_person_names_easy_02 “Miguel Santiago”, which are ordinary two-component names.

decisions.source_assessment: The English source “Janey Tsakos” is hard relative to the Easy controls because “Tsakos” is an uncommon surname with an initial consonant cluster and close decoys “Janey Tsomo” and “Jansen Tsakos”, plus pronunciation traps for both “Janey” and “Tsakos”. That is more difficult than Easy sources such as “Lisa Sandoval” in intake_person_names_easy_01 or “Susan Jenkins” in intake_person_names_easy_10.

hazards.evidence: “Jimena Zazo Chacón” has two family-name components, but in Spain this is a routine full-name shape and does not by itself create a hard capture problem relative to the Easy names.
hazards.resolving_clarification: “El nombre completo es Jimena Zazo Chacón; los apellidos son Zazo y Chacón.”

hazards.evidence: The possible spelling contrasts in “Zazo Chacón” are weak for Spain Spanish: “Zazo” with z is normally audibly distinct from “Saso”, and final n in “Chacón” is audible. Easy cases already include comparable or harder single-surname spelling issues such as “Susana Jiménez” versus “Susana Giménez” in intake_person_names_easy_10.
hazards.resolving_clarification: “Zazo se escribe Z-A-Z-O; Chacón lleva tilde en la o y termina en ene.”

decisions.comparison_to_easy: The localized “Jimena Zazo Chacón” is natural, but it is not clearly harder than the supplied Easy controls. intake_person_names_easy_05 “Jimena Macías” already has an accented surname; intake_person_names_easy_10 “Susana Jiménez” has a genuine j/g spelling ambiguity before i; and intake_person_names_easy_04 “Javier Herrera” includes double-r spelling guidance. The current hard case mainly adds a routine second Spanish surname without a strong ambiguous spelling, phonetic, or boundary hazard.
dependency_issues: The localized primary does not preserve the source-level difficulty: “Jimena Zazo Chacón” is a plausible Spanish full name, but its hazards are mostly routine and overlap with or are weaker than hazards already present in Easy comparators.

The decoys “Jimena Saso Chacón” and “Jimena Zazo Chacó” do not establish a strong hard capture challenge for Spain Spanish because z/s and final n are normally audible distinctions, not ambiguous capture points.
correction_instructions: Revise the localized primary to a credible Spain-Spanish full name that is naturally hard relative to the Easy set, with a concrete spelling, phonetic, or component-boundary hazard beyond merely having two routine surnames.
Keep the person-name scenario and lazy-omission protocol: the caller should know the full canonical name and initially provide only the given name, then provide the full family name when asked.
Update decoys so they test plausible Spanish written-name confusions or component boundaries for the revised name, not merely easy audible contrasts.
Update pronunciation examples to target the revised tokens and ensure each intentional distortion is audibly different in Spain Spanish.

decisions.source_assessment: The English source “Geoff Lifland-Fatigate” is independently hard: “Geoff” has a non-transparent spelling-to-sound mapping, “Lifland-Fatigate” is an uncommon hyphenated surname, and the source includes close decoys plus pronunciation traps for all three tokens. hazards.evidence: “Gonzalo Linde-Falcón” uses a compound hyphenated family name; after the scripted omission, the caller first says only “Gonzalo” and must later clarify “Linde-Falcón”.
hazards.resolving_clarification: “El nombre completo es Gonzalo Linde-Falcón; el apellido es Linde guion Falcón.”

hazards.evidence: “Falcón” contains an accented ó and final n; the decoy “Gonzalo Linde-Falcó” differs only by omitting the final n, so exact spelling matters.
hazards.resolving_clarification: “Falcón lleva tilde en la o y termina en ene: F-A-L-C-Ó-N.”

hazards.evidence: The boundary between “Linde” and “Falcón” must be captured with a hyphen; otherwise the answer could be entered as two separate surnames or with the wrong first surname, as in the decoy “Gonzalo Lindo-Falcón”.

decisions.comparison_to_easy: Compared with intake_person_names_easy_01 “Laura Sandoval”, intake_person_names_easy_02 “Miguel Santiago”, and intake_person_names_easy_07 “Sandra Cortés”, this case has a compound hyphenated surname and an accented final component. decisions.source_assessment: The English source plate "L8T 4B0G" is not just a simple numeric block plus letters: it mixes letters and digits inside both chunks and includes a digit 0 whose instructed speech is "oh", creating an O/zero capture hazard not present in easy source plates such as intake_codes_easy_01 "678-LSB", intake_codes_easy_04 "360-CKS", or intake_codes_easy_05 "413-DLT".

hazards.evidence: Native written value "O-0848-BG" contains province letter "O" immediately before a digit block beginning with "0"; if heard casually, the first two rounded-vowel items can be confused as letter O versus digit cero.
hazards.resolving_clarification: "Es letra O de Oviedo, guion, cero ocho cuatro ocho, guion, be ge."

hazards.evidence: In "O-0848-BG", the boundary between province code "O" and the numeric block "0848" matters; the decoy "O-8048-BG" has the same characters except the leading zero is not in the same position.
hazards.resolving_clarification: "Después del guion va primero un cero y luego ocho cuatro ocho: O-0848-BG."

decisions.comparison_to_easy: Compared with the supplied Easy plates intake_codes_easy_01 "6789 LSB", intake_codes_easy_04 "3604 CKS", and intake_codes_easy_05 "4137 DLT", this localized plate has an extra letter-vs-digit O/0 distinction at the province/numeric boundary and a leading zero whose position must be captured. The Easy member IDs may include zeros, but they do not require distinguishing a province letter O from an adjacent digit 0 in a local plate shape.

decisions.source_assessment: The English source "F0N 2V4B" mixes letters and digits in short chunks and has a digit 0 instructed to be spoken as "oh", so a listener must distinguish letter-like and digit-like material. This is harder than easy source plates such as intake_codes_easy_01 "678-LSB", intake_codes_easy_04 "360-CKS", and intake_codes_easy_05 "413-DLT", whose numeric and letter blocks are cleaner.

hazards.evidence: Native written value "O-2047-FN" contains the province letter "O" and also the digit "0" in "2047"; the initial letter and the zero in the digit block must not be normalized to the same character.
hazards.resolving_clarification: "La primera es letra O, y en los números es dos cero cuatro siete: O-2047-FN."

hazards.evidence: The digit block "2047" may be heard as a grouped number, but the exact sequence has to be "2-0-4-7"; the decoy "O-2407-FN" swaps the zero and four positions.
hazards.resolving_clarification: "El bloque central es dos, cero, cuatro, siete; no dos, cuatro, cero, siete."

decisions.comparison_to_easy: The Easy plates intake_codes_easy_01 "6789 LSB", intake_codes_easy_04 "3604 CKS", and intake_codes_easy_05 "4137 DLT" are local plate-like number-plus-letter strings without a province-letter O plus internal zero contrast. This hard case adds both the O/0 distinction and an order-sensitive zero inside "2047".

decisions.source_assessment: The English source VIN "WVGWYR174DT698437" is a 17-character mixed alphanumeric identifier with letters interleaved with digit groups; its decoys differ in internal digits, so exact capture is required. This is materially harder than the Easy controls, which are mostly short plates or MBR numeric IDs such as intake_codes_easy_02 "MBR-531954-80" and intake_codes_easy_06 "MBR-549539-93".

hazards.evidence: Native value "WVGWYR174DT698437" combines an initial six-letter block "WVGWYR", digit block "174", letters "DT", and digit block "698437"; losing a boundary or skipping one component changes the VIN.
hazards.resolving_clarification: "Va por bloques: W V G W Y R, luego 174, luego D T, y termina en 698437."

hazards.evidence: The initial sequence "WVGWYR" contains "W" and "V" close together; in Spanish "uve doble" followed by "uve" can be mis-captured if the listener does not record each letter separately.
hazards.resolving_clarification: "Empieza con uve doble, uve, ge, uve doble, ye, erre: WVGWYR."

hazards.evidence: The final digits "698437" are long enough to be chunked differently, and the decoys "...608447" and "...628467" show that internal zero/two/eight/four/six positions matter.
hazards.resolving_clarification: "El final es seis nueve ocho cuatro tres siete, escrito 698437."

decisions.comparison_to_easy: Unlike intake_codes_easy_02 through intake_codes_easy_10, which are MBR plus numeric groups, and unlike the Easy plates intake_codes_easy_01, intake_codes_easy_04, and intake_codes_easy_05, this VIN requires preserving several alternating letter and digit components, including the W/V spelling contrast and exact internal digit sequence.

decisions.source_assessment: The English source "MBR-Z9R0Q0V0-21" is an alternating alphanumeric member ID, not a normal numeric MBR ID. hazards.evidence: Native value "MBR-Z9R0Q0V0-21" alternates letters and digits in "Z9R0Q0V0"; the decoy "MBR-9ZR0Q0V0-51" shows that the first two components must be captured as Z then 9, not 9 then Z.

hazards.evidence: The middle block "R0Q0V0" contains letters "R", "Q", "V" separated by zeros; a listener must not treat the zeros as letter O or merge them into the letter names.
hazards.resolving_clarification: "Es erre, cero, cu, cero, uve, cero: R0Q0V0."

hazards.evidence: The full value "MBR-Z9R0Q0V0-21" has prefix, alphanumeric core, and final numeric suffix; the final "21" must remain separate from the alphanumeric core.
hazards.resolving_clarification: "Completo: MBR, guion, Z9R0Q0V0, guion, veintiuno."

decisions.comparison_to_easy: The Easy member IDs intake_codes_easy_02 to intake_codes_easy_10 use the same MBR prefix but then mostly numeric blocks, sometimes with zeros or repeated digits. This hard case adds a local natural letter-by-letter alphanumeric core with order-sensitive letter/digit boundaries and repeated zeros.

decisions.source_assessment: The English source "MBR-T7Q2Z8N0-62" is an alternating alphanumeric member ID with multiple letter/digit boundaries and a Z spelling instruction. This is harder than Easy numeric MBR controls such as intake_codes_easy_06 "MBR-549539-93", intake_codes_easy_08 "MBR-538988-27", and intake_codes_easy_10 "MBR-517886-89".

hazards.evidence: Native value "MBR-T7Q2Z8N0-62" begins the core with "T7"; the decoy "MBR-7TQ2Z8N0-36" demonstrates that the first letter/digit order is a capture hazard.
hazards.resolving_clarification: "Después de MBR va te, siete; no siete, te."
